question: How can concrete construction become circular?

answer.answer:
Circular concrete rests on two things: joints that can be taken apart again and data that follows the component. The one cited requirement for circular construction/DfDisAssembly (VA15) is traceable/linked data (VA9), and what it delivers downstream is material and energy saving and reduced CO2 and waste (VA4); monolithic and glued jointing is named as the obstacle, so reversible connections, and by extension precast and modular (PR5) component logic, are the lever. Circularity is thin in the record: 8 of the 50 coded cases draw on VA15 against 26 for VA9, and every deployed concrete process in front of me was adopted for cost, labour, quality, safety, digital, regulation or market, none for circularity. Expect certification to be the binding constraint, since regulatory/legal concern (RI18) is a stated requirement of both additive manufacturing (PR3) and on-site digital fabrication (PR8).

**The cited path, end to end**

VA15 "Circular construction/DfDisAssembly" (Value) carries exactly one inbound and one outbound dependency edge, and 8 of the 50 coded cases draw on it [1], so the path below is the whole of what the literature has connected to it.

Upstream: traceable/linked data (VA9) enables circular construction/DfDisAssembly (VA15), because component data and material passports make recovery and reuse economically viable [2], backed by peer-reviewed evidence and carried by 5 of the 50 coded cases [1]. VA9 itself is much more widely present, drawn on by 26 of the 50 coded cases [1], and it also mitigates increased cost/investment uncertainty (RI3), because material passports reduce uncertainty about the circular potential and economics of disassembled elements, carried by 7 of the 50 [1]. So the tracking layer is already common practice in the record; what is rare is turning it to circular ends.

Downstream: circular construction/DfDisAssembly (VA15) enables material/energy saving/reduce CO2/waste (VA4), on the mechanism that glued and monolithic joints limit salvage potential while reversible connection design under DfDisAssembly enables material recovery [3], peer-reviewed and carried by 6 of the 50 [1]. That sentence is the practical instruction for concrete: cast-in-place monolithic work forecloses recovery, so the circular route runs through demountable connections. VA4 is drawn on by 15 of the 50 coded cases [1].

**What sits beside it, as correlation only**

Within the cut of VA15's co-occurrences given here, and these are statistical, not asserted dependencies: material testing (PR10) at weight 8, integrate supply chain (VA14) at 7, modularisation (PR5), DfMA for DFAB process (PR9), early contractor involvement (CO11) and increased cost/investment uncertainty (RI3) at 6 each, bespoke/customised design (AT1) at 5, subtractive manufacturing (PR7) and CNC machines (RE7) at 4, and increased material usage/waste (RI16) at 3, out of 125 co-occurring enablers in total [4]. Material testing appearing alongside every one of the eight VA15 cases is consistent with recovered or novel concrete needing verification, but it is a correlation and the literature has not connected the two.

**The deployed record**

The concrete processes retrieved here are: RP9, adopted to address cost and market, performing assembly, concrete work and precast on the structural core, deployed off-site at technology readiness level 9 [5]; RP16, adopted to address cost, performing assembly, concrete work, precast, rebar and steelwork off-site at technology readiness level 9 [6]; RP1, adopted to address cost, labor and integration, performing 3D printing and concrete work as a mobile robot off-site, on site and outdoors at technology readiness level 8 [7]; RP47, addressing digital, cost, quality and labor through 3D printing, concrete work, shotcrete and surface treatment at technology readiness level 7 [8]; and RP15, adopted to address regulation, performing 3D printing, assembly and concrete work off-site at technology readiness level 7 [9]. The context names no firm behind any of these records, and it does not link any of them to VA15, so I cannot say that any deployed concrete process here exhibits circular construction or design for disassembly. The precast, off-site cases at readiness level 9, RP9 and RP16, are the ones whose component logic is closest to the reversible-jointing mechanism, but that is an inference from what they fabricate, not a coded circularity claim.

**What to watch**

Certification is a stated dependency, not an afterthought. Additive manufacturing (PR3) depends on regulatory/legal concern (RI18), since 3D printed concrete walls require certification against acceptance criteria for structural strength, fire safety and durability [10], and on-site DFAB (PR8) likewise depends on RI18, with on-site 3D concrete printing proceeding via an alternative-means approval pathway [11], both on standards evidence and each carried by 2 of the 50 coded cases [1]. Prefabrication/off-site (PR2) also depends on RI18, on the ground that a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability, carried by 10 of the 50 [1], which is the same traceability requirement that VA9 supplies, arriving from the compliance side. RI18 is drawn on by 12 of the 50 coded cases [1].

Two limits on this answer. Retrieval read the question through VA15 alone, so what is reported is the circularity value and its single cited path, not everything the record holds about concrete. And the cited dependency layer is uneven by design: 100 edges touch 68 of the 140 enablers, and 48% of Values carry no cited edge at all [1], so the absence of further cited routes into circularity reflects what the literature has connected rather than what the cases contain.

**Deployed evidence.** Selected by filtering the coded records, not by similarity. 12 records in the graph carry Concrete as their material; all are listed below.
- RP1, adopted to address cost, labor, integration; performs 3d printing, concrete work; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP11, adopted to address digital; performs assembly, concrete work, rebar, steelwork; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP15, adopted to address regulation; performs 3d printing, assembly, concrete work; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, off-site; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP16, adopted to address cost; performs assembly, concrete work, precast, rebar, steelwork; works on the structural core; deployed off-site; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP19, adopted to address labor; performs concrete work, finishing, surface treatment; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP36, adopted to address safety, labor; performs cleaning, inspection; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP37, adopted to address digital, quality, safety, labor; performs inspection; works on the building envelope, the facade, or curtain wall; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP40, adopted to address safety, labor; performs assembly, rebar, steelwork; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP43, adopted to address safety, labor; performs surface treatment; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP46, adopted to address digital, quality, labor; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP47, adopted to address digital, cost, quality, labor; performs 3d printing, concrete work, shotcrete, surface treatment; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP9, adopted to address cost, market; performs assembly, concrete work, precast; works on the structural core; deployed off-site; at technology readiness level 9.
